summary:
Volgograd Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and no oblast-level deviation from that framework appears in the sources. The baseline is set by the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025; assessment updated 11 June 2025): same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and no specific legal protections exist.

Under that framework, the 'gay propaganda' statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to 4 years in prison. The Supreme Court's designation of the International LGBT Movement as extremist carries 2 to 6 years for participating and 6 to 10 years for organising.

Volgograd itself appears in the record. A court in Volgograd imposed detention and subsequent deportation on a transgender sex worker, a Tajik citizen, over her online posts — an outcome that shows how the propaganda and extremism provisions reach foreign nationals resident in the oblast and end in removal.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) recorded 101 convictions for extremism tied to the International LGBT Movement following the 2023 designation. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison. A further 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols, with participants of the designated movement facing up to 12 years in prison.

Across Russia between 2022 and 2024, at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

Care access carries a measurable risk of being outed. Survey data place the Southern Federal District, which includes Volgograd Oblast, at 27% for discrimination from healthcare providers who knew the patient's sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The national situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the expanded 'propaganda' law criminalises public expression that merely 'justifies' gender transition.

Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement has accelerated. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two preceding years. The Guardian documented the speed of the post-designation crackdown on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is also documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Residents of Volgograd Oblast live under the same bans as the rest of Russia: legal gender recognition and the legal route to gender-affirming care were closed in 2023, and gender transition is not recognised for the purposes of marriage or official documents.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility, and Human Rights Watch separately recorded one person dying by suicide in pretrial detention between January 2024 and June 2025.

The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation, framing how the designation is experienced in daily life.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records oblast-level hate-crime statistics, police conduct complaints, or physical-assault data for Volgograd Oblast, so violence risk there is inferred from the national pattern rather than measured locally.

The survey figure of 27% healthcare discrimination is reported for the Southern Federal District as a whole; the underlying sample, methodology and year of fieldwork are not stated in the sources available here.

Whether article 20.3 symbol-display proceedings or International LGBT Movement participation charges have been brought in Volgograd Oblast specifically is not documented beyond the single Volgograd court case involving detention and deportation.

Facilities, support services and safe premises for transgender visitors within the oblast are not sourced in this inventory.
